blogs.title: When Neuro-Behçet's Presents at the Same Time as Systemic Disease: A Diagnostic Red Flag
blogs.description: Neurological involvement in Behçet's disease typically emerges years after the initial diagnosis, making concurrent presentation of systemic BD and neuro-BD a clinical rarity (occurring in <5% of patients). This post explores the diagnostic challenge when CNS symptoms appear at or before the onset of classic mucocutaneous findings, as occurred in this case where genital ulcers did not appear until day 5. We discuss the International Criteria for Behçet's Disease (ICBD) scoring system, the role of HLA-B51 testing (supportive but not diagnostic), and why clinicians should maintain suspicion for neuro-BD even when the full clinical picture hasn't yet declared itself. The post also addresses how the absence of complete mucocutaneous findings early in the presentation led to a broad and arguably unfocused diagnostic workup, and how recognizing patterns earlier could streamline the diagnostic process.

blogs.title: A Normal Brain MRI Does Not Exclude Acute Neuro-Behçet's Disease
blogs.description: Acute neuro-BD most commonly presents with meningoencephalitis and parenchymal lesions, particularly in the brainstem. However, this case demonstrates a critical teaching point: acute neuro-BD can present as aseptic meningitis with a completely normal brain MRI, especially in the early phase of disease. This post examines the radiographic pitfalls in diagnosing neuro-BD, the spectrum of MRI findings (from normal to characteristic brainstem/thalamic lesions), and the importance of CSF analysis in establishing the diagnosis of CNS inflammation when imaging is unrevealing. We discuss the CSF profile expected in neuro-BD (lymphocytic pleocytosis, elevated protein, aseptic pattern) and how to systematically exclude infectious, neoplastic, and other inflammatory etiologies before settling on a diagnosis of neuro-BD. The post also explores why early MRI may be normal and when repeat imaging should be considered.

blogs.title: SIADH as a Complication of CNS Inflammation: The IL-6 Connection and What It Means for Your Hyponatremic Patient
blogs.description: This post examines the proposed link between acute neuro-BD and SIADH, exploring the pathophysiological mechanism by which CNS inflammation may dysregulate ADH secretion. We review the role of interleukin-6 (IL-6)—a cytokine known to stimulate ADH release and frequently elevated in both BD and neuroinflammatory conditions—as a potential mediator connecting neuro-BD to SIADH. Although IL-6 was not directly measured in this case, the markedly elevated CRP may reflect IL-6-driven inflammation. We also discuss the broader principle that any CNS inflammatory process (meningitis, encephalitis, autoimmune neuroinflammation) can trigger SIADH, review the diagnostic criteria for SIADH (hypo-osmolality, inappropriately concentrated urine, euvolemia, elevated urinary sodium, normal adrenal and thyroid function), and consider when clinicians should suspect that hyponatremia in a neurologically ill patient is more than a lab abnormality—it may be a clue to the severity and extent of CNS inflammation.

blogs.title: Hiccups and Rhabdomyolysis: The Underappreciated Clinical Clues to Profound Hyponatremia
blogs.description: Persistent hiccups and elevated creatine kinase (rhabdomyolysis) are two underrecognized manifestations of severe hyponatremia that featured prominently in this case. This post reviews the evidence linking intractable hiccups to hyponatremia-induced neurogenic dysfunction and discusses why this symptom is frequently dismissed or attributed to other causes in the emergency and inpatient settings. We also examine rhabdomyolysis as a complication of profound hyponatremia—its pathophysiology (osmotic shifts damaging muscle cell membranes), its overlap with other causes of CK elevation (inflammatory myositis in BD, metabolic causes), and why it is often missed because CK is not routinely checked in patients with hyponatremia. The post provides a practical framework for evaluating unexpected symptoms in hyponatremic patients and emphasizes that these manifestations should prompt clinicians to consider the severity of the electrolyte disturbance as a clinical emergency, not just a laboratory value.

blogs.title: Colchicine Monotherapy for Acute Neuro-Behçet's: Challenging the Steroid-First Paradigm
blogs.description: Corticosteroids are considered the mainstay of treatment for acute neuro-BD, and systematic reviews have shown that colchicine alone is ineffective for neuro-BD, with immunosuppressive agents generally required. Yet this case achieved complete resolution of mucocutaneous symptoms, neurological manifestations, and SIADH with colchicine monotherapy alone—no systemic corticosteroids or other immunosuppressants were used. This post critically examines this apparent paradox: Was this spontaneous resolution of a self-limiting meningoencephalitis, or does colchicine's mechanism (inhibiting neutrophil migration and suppressing IL-1β and IL-6) offer genuine therapeutic benefit in mild acute neuro-BD? We review the evidence base for colchicine in BD (primarily for mucocutaneous disease), the limited but intriguing data on spontaneous resolution in neuro-BD presenting solely with meningoencephalitis, and the potential role for colchicine as a steroid-sparing agent in select neuro-BD patients. We also discuss the clinical decision-making around when to escalate from colchicine to corticosteroids or immunosuppression, and what factors (parenchymal involvement, severity of CNS inflammation, presence of complications like SIADH) should influence that threshold.

blogs.title: Diagnostic Parsimony in Complex Presentations: Lessons from a Case That Triggered an Indiscriminate Workup
blogs.description: This case illustrates a common pitfall in diagnostic reasoning: when the initial presentation is non-specific (fever, headache, hyponatremia) and the diagnosis is uncertain, clinicians may resort to broad, indiscriminate testing. In this case, autoimmune panels, serum ACE, soluble IL-2 receptor, and multiple viral/bacterial CSF panels were ordered as part of an exclusion-based approach rather than being driven by specific clinical suspicion. While the final diagnosis of neuro-BD was eventually established through careful clinical observation (appearance of genital ulcers on day 5) and application of the ICBD criteria, much of the early workup was non-contributory. This post examines the tension between thoroughness and diagnostic parsimony, discusses the limitations of screening tests like ACE (poor sensitivity for sarcoidosis) and sIL-2R (non-specific mild elevations in inflammation), and proposes a framework for when to broaden vs. narrow the differential diagnosis. We also explore the cognitive biases that drive over-testing (diagnostic uncertainty, anchoring on life-threatening but unlikely diagnoses) and how a pattern-recognition approach to mucocutaneous findings could have shortened the diagnostic timeline.
